claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native pre-exposure oxide film.
Temperature, oxygen, water vapor, and chloride concentration govern formation of the initial oxide film on Q235 steel.
Oxidation kinetics on Q235 steel are slower at room temperature than at 80–100°C.
Room-temperature exposure favors formation of a compact, adherent, and continuous oxide film on Q235 steel.
A compact protective oxide can act as a diffusion barrier and hinder further oxidation.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation of Q235 steel.
At elevated temperature, chloride ions promote defects, porosity, and cracking in the oxide film on Q235 steel.
A porous or cracked oxide film accelerates ingress of water and oxygen.
Loss of oxide-film integrity promotes corrosion-related degradation.
Q235 samples exposed at 80–100°C under high humidity and high chloride will corrode faster than samples exposed at approximately 25°C under otherwise similar conditions.
Elevated-temperature, high-humidity, high-chloride samples will exhibit greater weight loss, more pitting, and less-uniform oxide layers.
Chloride-limited controls will exhibit less corrosion than high-chloride samples.
Q235 steel held at room temperature in an inert or low-chloride, moderate-humidity environment will show minimal corrosion and a uniform protective oxide.
The controlled study varies temperature, humidity, and chloride level while holding oxygen partial pressure constant.
Weight loss, EIS, SEM, and XPS can be used to compare corrosion rate, oxide-film defects, morphology, and composition among exposure groups.
The hypothesis is falsified if elevated-temperature, high-chloride, high-humidity samples show neither significantly higher corrosion nor more defective oxide films than both comparison groups.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the material 'pre-exposed Q235 steel,' whereas the initial-state and boundary fields describe pre-exposure, as-received steel. These denote different exposure histories unless 'pre-exposed' is a wording error.

The intervention and conditions state that oxygen partial pressure is fixed, but the boundary field lists oxygen partial pressure among the variables, leaving its controlled-versus-varied status inconsistent.
The intervention requires constant high oxygen partial pressure, while one proposed baseline is an inert environment. An inert baseline cannot simultaneously maintain the same high oxygen level.
